assessment_style: freeCodeCamp-style: progressive MCQ checkpoints (theory, logic, syntax) per lesson, each lesson capped by an applied coding challenge; module ends with a capstone project synthesizing all 10 lessons
note_on_relationship_to_existing_quiz: This assessment is a SEPARATE, additive practice layer. It does not duplicate the 3 quiz questions or 1 coding_quest already embedded in each lesson of the enriched module JSON. It is designed to be taken independently as a standalone practice/certification pass.

theory_mcq.question: What is the fundamental structural difference between a static array and a dynamic array?
options: Static arrays are always faster to read from than dynamic arrays

A static array is a fixed-size contiguous memory block that cannot grow; a dynamic array is a higher-level structure that APPEARS resizable but is internally backed by a static array that gets reallocated and copied when capacity runs out
Dynamic arrays don't use contiguous memory at all
There is no real difference; the terms are interchangeable
theory_mcq.explanation: Static arrays have a fixed capacity set at allocation. Dynamic arrays (JS Array, Python list, Java ArrayList) simulate resizability by internally allocating a new, larger static array and copying elements over when the current one fills up — the resizing is hidden from the programmer.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the doubling strategy (rather than growing by a fixed increment) guarantee O(1) amortized push cost?
options: Doubling has no effect on amortized cost
Doubling ensures the total copies across n pushes is bounded by 2n (a result proven via amortized analysis in L1-M01), keeping the average cost per push constant regardless of how many pushes occur
Doubling makes every individual push exactly the same speed
This is purely a JavaScript-specific quirk with no general justification
theory_mcq.explanation: This lesson explicitly revisits L1-M01 L7's amortized analysis proof: doubling capacity bounds total resize-copy work at roughly 2n across n pushes, which is what produces O(1) amortized cost per push — a fixed increment strategy would NOT achieve this bound.

theory_mcq.question: What is the memory cost ('overhead') of the dynamic array's resizing strategy, and when is it worst?
options: There is no memory overhead with dynamic arrays
Immediately after a resize, the array is half empty (capacity is double what's actually used) — this over-allocation is the trade-off for amortized O(1) push performance
The overhead only occurs the very first time an array is created
Memory overhead only matters for arrays larger than 1 million elements
theory_mcq.explanation: Right after doubling capacity, only half the newly-allocated space is filled — this is the explicit memory cost the lesson identifies as the trade-off for achieving amortized O(1) push, distinct from the time-complexity benefit.

logic_mcq.question: Using the lesson's DynamicArray class, if capacity starts at 1 and doubles on each resize, what is the capacity sequence as 5 elements are pushed (1 by 1)?
options: 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 (capacity never changes)

1, 2, 4, 4, 8 — capacity AFTER each push: push 1 has length=0, capacity=1 (not equal, no resize, capacity stays 1); push 2 has length=1=capacity=1 (resize to 2); push 3 has length=2=capacity=2 (resize to 4); push 4 has length=3<capacity=4 (no resize); push 5 has length=4=capacity=4 (resize to 8)
5, 5, 5, 5, 5 (capacity is set to final size immediately)
1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (capacity grows by 1 each push)
logic_mcq.explanation: Step-by-step trace (verified by execution): push(0): length=0, capacity=1 -- NOT equal, so no resize; after storing, length=1, capacity=1. push(1): length=1, capacity=1 -- EQUAL, resize triggers, capacity becomes 2; after storing, length=2, capacity=2. push(2): length=2, capacity=2 -- EQUAL, resize triggers, capacity becomes 4; after storing, length=3, capacity=4. push(3): length=3, capacity=4 -- not equal, no resize; after storing, length=4, capacity=4. push(4): length=4, capacity=4 -- EQUAL, resize triggers, capacity becomes 8; after storing, length=5, capacity=8. Capacity after each of the 5 pushes: 1, 2, 4, 4, 8.

logic_mcq.question: A developer knows in advance they need to store exactly 10,000 elements, but pushes them one at a time into an empty dynamic array without pre-allocating. Compared to pre-allocating with `new Array(10000)`, what's the practical consequence?
options: No difference at all — both approaches perform identically

The non-pre-allocated version will trigger multiple resize-and-copy operations along the way (still amortized O(1) per push overall, but with real, avoidable copy work), while pre-allocation eliminates ALL resize overhead entirely since capacity never needs to grow
Pre-allocation is always slower because it wastes memory upfront
Pushing one at a time is illegal in JavaScript
logic_mcq.explanation: The lesson explicitly notes that pre-allocating when the final size is known 'eliminates all resize overhead entirely' — while the incremental approach still achieves the same amortized O(1) bound, it does real (if amortized-cheap) copy work along the way that pre-allocation avoids completely.

syntax_mcq.question: What does `new Int32Array(10)` create, and how does it differ from a plain JavaScript array `[]`?
options: It creates a resizable array identical to a plain array
It creates a fixed-size, typed array of exactly 10 32-bit integers with a fixed memory footprint that cannot grow — closer in behavior to a true static array, unlike a plain JS Array which is dynamic
It creates an array of strings
It has no meaningful difference from a regular array
syntax_mcq.explanation: Int32Array is a TypedArray with a fixed length set at construction — it cannot be resized afterward, making it a closer JavaScript analog to a true static array, in contrast to the standard dynamic Array type.

syntax_mcq.question: In `new Array(n).fill(0)`, what does `.fill(0)` accomplish?
options: It removes all elements from the array
It sets every element in the newly created array (of length n) to the value 0, ensuring the array is fully populated rather than containing empty/undefined slots
It sorts the array
It doubles the array's length
syntax_mcq.explanation: `new Array(n)` alone creates an array with n empty slots (not actual 0 values). `.fill(0)` populates every one of those slots with the value 0, which matters because some array methods behave differently on empty slots versus actual values.

coding_challenges.title: Build a Capacity-Tracking Dynamic Array From Scratch
coding_challenges.problem_statement: Implement a TrackedDynamicArray class that mirrors the lesson's DynamicArray implementation but additionally exposes its internal capacity and resize count, then write a function comparing total resize operations between pre-allocated and non-pre-allocated approaches for the same final size.
requirements: Implement `TrackedDynamicArray` with `push(val)`, `get(i)`, and public `capacity`/`length`/`resizeCount` properties, doubling capacity on resize starting from capacity=1

Implement `compareApproaches(n)` that returns `{ incrementalResizes, preallocatedResizes }` — incrementalResizes is the resizeCount after pushing n elements one at a time into a TrackedDynamicArray; preallocatedResizes should be 0 (since pre-allocation avoids resizing)

test_cases.input: (() => { const d = new TrackedDynamicArray(); for(let i=0;i<5;i++) d.push(i); return d.resizeCount; })()
(() => { const d = new TrackedDynamicArray(); d.push(7); return d.get(0); })()

coding_challenges.complexity_analysis: push: O(1) amortized, O(n) worst case during a resize. resizeCount after n pushes is approximately ceil(log2(n)) since capacity doubles from 1 each time. For n=5: capacities 1->2->4->8, that's 3 resizes (matches test case). For n=100: capacities 1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128 -- 7 resizes to reach capacity >= 100.

hints.text: Mirror the lesson's DynamicArray push logic exactly, adding resizeCount++ inside the resize branch.
compareApproaches just needs to run n pushes through a fresh TrackedDynamicArray and read off resizeCount; preallocatedResizes is always 0 by definition.
resizeCount after n pushes follows ceil(log2(n)) when starting capacity=1 and doubling — verify your trace matches: n=5 -> 3 resizes, n=100 -> 7 resizes.

theory_mcq.question: Why is reading an array by index always O(1), regardless of array size or which index is accessed?
options: Because arrays are always small
Because the CPU computes the target memory address directly via base_address + index × element_size — a single arithmetic operation, with no searching required, regardless of array size or position
Because JavaScript caches every array element separately
Index reads are actually O(n), not O(1)
theory_mcq.explanation: This is the same address-calculation principle from L1-M01 L2: contiguous memory allows direct address computation for any index in constant time, independent of array size.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the lesson describe array insertion/deletion performance as an 'asymmetry — fast at the end, slow everywhere else'?
options: Because arrays behave randomly and unpredictably

Because inserting/deleting at the END requires no element shifting (O(1) amortized), while inserting/deleting anywhere else requires shifting all subsequent elements to maintain contiguity (O(n)) — this asymmetry is a direct consequence of how contiguous memory works
Because arrays are slower at the beginning than the middle
This asymmetry has been deprecated in modern array implementations
theory_mcq.explanation: End operations avoid shifting because no elements come after the modified position. Operations at the front or middle require shifting every subsequent element by one position to preserve contiguity — this structural cost is what motivates alternative structures (linked lists, deques) when frequent non-end insertion/deletion is needed.

logic_mcq.question: Given `arr.splice(1, 0, 15)` on `[10,20,30,40,50,60]` (6 elements), how many elements must be shifted to make room for the insertion at index 1?
options: 0 elements need to shift
5 elements (20,30,40,50,60) all shift one position to the right to make room for the new element at index 1
1 element shifts
All 6 elements including the new one are recreated from scratch
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's trace exactly: inserting at index 1 requires shifting every element from the old index 1 onward (20,30,40,50,60 — 5 elements) one position to the right to make room, giving O(n) cost for this operation.

logic_mcq.question: The lesson shows `badContains` using `arr.indexOf(t)` inside a loop over `targets`. If `arr` has n elements and `targets` has m elements, what is the overall time complexity of `badContains`, and why is it described as 'hidden quadratic'?
options: O(n + m), since each operation is considered separately

O(n × m), since the outer loop runs m times and EACH call to .indexOf() is itself an O(n) linear scan — the quadratic cost isn't obvious from reading the code because .indexOf() looks like a simple, fast built-in call
O(1), since .indexOf() is a built-in method
O(log(n × m))
logic_mcq.explanation: This is exactly the 'hidden quadratic' trap the lesson warns about: .indexOf() looks innocuous as a single method call, but it's actually an O(n) linear scan internally. Calling it m times inside a loop produces O(n×m) total work, which is easy to miss without knowing .indexOf()'s actual complexity.

logic_mcq.question: The lesson's fix, `goodContains`, converts `arr` to a Set first. What is its overall time complexity, and how does it compare to `badContains`?
options: Still O(n × m), no real improvement
O(n + m) — O(n) once to build the Set, then O(1) average-case per lookup across m targets — a significant improvement over badContains's O(n × m) when both n and m are large
O(n²) — worse than badContains
O(1) regardless of n or m
logic_mcq.explanation: Building the Set is a one-time O(n) cost. Each of the m lookups via .has() is then O(1) average-case, giving O(n + m) total — a substantial improvement over O(n × m) for large inputs, directly applying the Set-based optimization pattern from L1-M01.

syntax_mcq.question: What does `arr.splice(1, 1)` do to the array `[10,15,20,30,40,50]`?
options: Inserts a new element at index 1
Removes 1 element starting at index 1 (removes the value 15), then shifts all subsequent elements left by one position to fill the gap
Removes the entire array
Returns the element at index 1 without modifying the array
syntax_mcq.explanation: `splice(start, deleteCount)` with deleteCount=1 removes exactly 1 element beginning at the given start index — here removing 15 at index 1, then all later elements (20,30,40,50) shift one position left.

coding_challenges.title: Operation Cost Profiler for Array Methods
coding_challenges.problem_statement: Build a tool that empirically measures and confirms the complexity claims for core array operations by counting actual shift operations performed, then refactor a 'hidden quadratic' function into an optimal one.
requirements: Implement `insertAtWithShiftCount(arr, index, value)` that performs the insertion manually (not using splice) and returns the number of elements shifted
Implement `deleteAtWithShiftCount(arr, index)` that performs the deletion manually and returns the number of elements shifted
Refactor the lesson's `badContains(arr, targets)` into `goodContains(arr, targets)` using a Set, matching the lesson's optimization exactly
coding_challenges.complexity_analysis: insertAtWithShiftCount/deleteAtWithShiftCount: O(n) due to shifting, with shift count equal to (number of elements after the modified index). goodContains: O(n + m) total versus badContains's O(n × m), directly demonstrating the Set-based optimization's real-world impact.

hints.text: For insertAtWithShiftCount: grow the array by one slot, then shift each element from the end down to (but not including) the target index one position right.
For deleteAtWithShiftCount: shift each element after the target index one position left, then remove the now-duplicated last slot.
goodContains: const set = new Set(arr); return targets.filter(t => set.has(t)); — directly mirrors the lesson's fix.

theory_mcq.question: What is the key structural insight that allows the Two Pointer technique to replace an O(n²) nested loop with an O(n) single pass?
options: Two pointers always run twice as fast as one pointer

Two Pointers exploits a structural property of the problem (sortedness, symmetry, or monotonicity) to make an informed decision about which pointer to move at each step, covering all necessary cases in a single O(n) pass instead of exhaustively checking all pairs
Two Pointers only works on arrays smaller than 1000 elements
Two Pointers eliminates the need for any comparisons
theory_mcq.explanation: The lesson is explicit: a nested loop explores ALL pairs (O(n²)) because it has no information to skip unnecessary comparisons. Two Pointers uses problem structure (e.g., sorted order) to PROVABLY skip large portions of the search space, reaching O(n) with a single informed pass.

theory_mcq.question: What is the critical discipline the lesson emphasizes before coding a Two Pointer solution?
options: Always start with the right pointer at index 0
Proving to yourself WHY moving a specific pointer cannot miss the optimal answer, before coding — correctness depends on this reasoning, not on intuition or trial and error
Writing the code first and testing afterward
Two Pointer correctness never needs to be proven, it's always safe
theory_mcq.explanation: The lesson explicitly states this discipline: each pointer movement decision must be justified by a correctness argument (as demonstrated in the twoSumSorted proof: 'if sum < target, nums[left] is too small with ANY right partner, so moving left is safe'), not assumed to be correct by intuition.

logic_mcq.question: In `twoSumSorted`, why is it safe to move `left++` when `sum < target`, without risking missing the correct answer?
options: It isn't actually safe; this is a bug in the algorithm

If nums[left] + nums[right] is too small, then nums[left] paired with ANY value at or before the current right position would also be too small (since the array is sorted and right is already at its largest useful value for this left) — so nums[left] can never contribute to a valid answer with the current or any smaller right, making it safe to move past it
Moving left is just an arbitrary tie-breaking choice with no correctness justification
It's only safe if the array has no duplicate values
logic_mcq.explanation: This is the exact correctness proof given in the lesson: since the array is sorted, if the current pair sums too small, nums[left] is definitively 'too small' to pair with anything at the current right position or smaller — so advancing left cannot skip over the true answer.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `removeDuplicatesSorted([0,0,1,1,1,2,2,3])`. What is the returned value, and what does it represent?
options: Returns 8, the original array length
Returns 4, the count of unique values (0,1,2,3) — the function partitions the array so the first 4 positions hold the unique values in order, and returns this count as the 'length of unique prefix'
Returns 0, an error case
Returns the array itself, not a number
logic_mcq.explanation: Following the slow/fast pointer trace: slow only advances (and writes) when a NEW unique value is found by fast. For this input, the 4 unique values (0,1,2,3) get written to indices 0-3, and slow ends at index 3, so slow+1=4 is returned — matching the lesson's stated result exactly.

logic_mcq.question: What is the time and space complexity of `isPalindrome(s)` as written in the lesson, including the cost of `s.toLowerCase().replace(...)`?
options: O(1) time, O(1) space

O(n) time, O(n) space — the toLowerCase/replace operations create a new cleaned string (O(n) time and space), and the subsequent two-pointer scan is O(n) time with O(1) additional space, but the cleaned-string copy dominates the space cost
O(n²) time, O(n) space
O(n) time, O(1) space, with no extra memory used anywhere
logic_mcq.explanation: The lesson explicitly states 'Time: O(n) Space: O(n) for cleaned string' for this version, while also noting a possible O(1) space optimization (skipping non-alphanumeric characters in-place rather than creating a new cleaned string) as an alternative.

syntax_mcq.question: In `[arr[left], arr[right]] = [arr[right], arr[left]];`, what JavaScript feature is being used, and what does this line do?
options: This is invalid JavaScript syntax
This is array destructuring assignment, used here to swap the values at indices left and right in a single, concise statement without needing a temporary variable
It creates two new arrays
It deletes both elements
syntax_mcq.explanation: Destructuring assignment lets you swap two values in one line: the right-hand side `[arr[right], arr[left]]` is evaluated first into a temporary array, then destructured into arr[left] and arr[right] respectively — a common, idiomatic JS swap pattern.

syntax_mcq.question: What does the regular expression `/[^a-z0-9]/g` match, as used in `s.toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9]/g, '')`?
options: It matches only lowercase letters and digits, removing them

It matches any character that is NOT a lowercase letter or digit (the `^` inside `[]` negates the character class), and the `g` flag applies this globally, removing all such characters to leave only alphanumeric characters
It matches only spaces
It matches the entire string regardless of content
syntax_mcq.explanation: Inside a character class, `^` negates the set — `[^a-z0-9]` matches any character that is NOT a lowercase letter or digit. Combined with `.replace(..., '')` and the global `g` flag, this strips out all punctuation/spaces, leaving only the cleaned alphanumeric content for palindrome comparison.

coding_challenges.title: Two Pointer Pattern Suite: Container With Most Water
coding_challenges.problem_statement: Given an array of non-negative integers representing wall heights, find two walls that, together with the x-axis, form a container holding the most water. Implement both a brute-force O(n²) version and an optimal O(n) Two Pointer version, then write your own correctness justification as a comment for why the pointer movement is safe.
requirements: Implement `maxAreaBrute(heights)` checking all pairs, O(n²) time
Implement `maxAreaOptimal(heights)` using the opposite-ends Two Pointer pattern, O(n) time, O(1) space
Write a comment proving why, at each step, moving the pointer at the SHORTER wall (not the taller one) cannot miss the optimal answer
Implement `isPalindromeTwoPointer(s)` applying the opposite-ends pattern for palindrome checking (case-insensitive, ignoring non-alphanumeric characters)

test_cases.input: isPalindromeTwoPointer('A man, a plan, a canal: Panama')

coding_challenges.complexity_analysis: maxAreaBrute: O(n²) time, O(1) space. maxAreaOptimal: O(n) time, O(1) space. isPalindromeTwoPointer: O(n) time, O(n) space (due to the cleaned string copy, matching the lesson's stated complexity).

hints.text: Container area = min(height[i], height[j]) * (j - i) — the shorter wall always determines the water level.

For maxAreaOptimal: always move the pointer at the SHORTER wall inward, since the taller wall could still potentially pair with a later wall to produce a larger area, but the shorter wall has already given its best possible result with the current opposite pointer.
isPalindromeTwoPointer directly mirrors the lesson's isPalindrome implementation: clean the string first, then apply the opposite-ends two-pointer comparison.

theory_mcq.question: Why is the Sliding Window pattern O(n) overall, even though it involves what looks like nested logic (an outer loop with an inner while loop in the variable-size version)?
options: Because the inner while loop never actually executes

Because across the ENTIRE execution, each element enters the window (via the right pointer) and leaves the window (via the left pointer) AT MOST ONCE — so even though there are two loop constructs, the TOTAL combined work across both is bounded by O(n), not O(n²)
Because sliding window only works on arrays smaller than 100 elements
It is actually O(n²), and the lesson's claim of O(n) is incorrect
theory_mcq.explanation: This is the precise amortized-style argument the lesson gives: although there's a while loop nested inside a for loop, the LEFT pointer only ever moves forward and can move at most n times total across the entire algorithm's execution — so the combined cost of all the inner while loop iterations, summed across every outer iteration, is bounded by O(n), not O(n) per outer iteration.

theory_mcq.question: What signal in a problem statement indicates a FIXED-size window is needed, versus a VARIABLE-size window?
options: Fixed windows are used for string problems, variable windows only for arrays

If the problem specifies an exact window size k upfront (e.g., 'subarray of size k'), use a fixed window; if the problem asks for the longest/shortest contiguous segment satisfying some CONDITION (size not given upfront), use a variable window that expands/shrinks based on that condition
There is no meaningful distinction; both patterns are identical
Fixed windows are always faster than variable windows
theory_mcq.explanation: The lesson's explicit recognition signal: 'subarray/substring of exactly size k' maps to fixed window, while 'longest/shortest satisfying condition X' maps to variable window — this distinction determines which implementation pattern to apply.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `maxSumSubarray([2,1,5,1,3,2], k=3)` window by window. What sums does each window produce, and what's the final answer?
options: Only one window is checked: [2,1,5]=8 -> max=8
logic_mcq.explanation: This matches the lesson's exact worked trace: the windows of size 3 are [2,1,5]=8, [1,5,1]=7, [5,1,3]=9, [1,3,2]=6, giving a maximum of 9.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `lengthOfLongestSubstring('pwwkew')`. At what point does the window first need to shrink (the while loop trigger), and why?
options: It never needs to shrink for this input
When right reaches the second 'w' (index 2), charSet already contains 'w' from index 1, triggering the while loop to remove characters from the left until the duplicate 'w' is cleared from the window
The window shrinks at every single step regardless of duplicates
It shrinks only at the very end of the string
logic_mcq.explanation: Tracing 'pwwkew': right=0 adds 'p', right=1 adds 'w' (window 'pw'), right=2 finds 'w' already in charSet, triggering the while loop to shrink: remove 'p' (left=1), still has 'w' in window? No wait — remove 'p' from index 0, left becomes 1, charSet now has just 'w' from index 1, but right=2 is also 'w' — so it continues shrinking, removing 'w' at index 1, left becomes 2, now charSet is empty, exits while loop, adds 'w' at index 2. This is the exact point where shrinking is first triggered, due to a duplicate 'w' entering the window.

logic_mcq.question: For `lengthOfLongestSubstring('bbbbb')`, what is the final result, and what does this reveal about the algorithm's behavior on inputs with NO variety?
options: Result: 5, since the whole string counts

Result: 1 — every time right encounters another 'b' (already in the window), the while loop immediately shrinks left until just the new 'b' remains in the window, since with all-identical characters, the window can never hold more than 1 character without a duplicate
Result: 0, since the function fails on repeated characters
This input causes an infinite loop
logic_mcq.explanation: This matches the lesson's stated result exactly: for an all-identical-character string, the window must shrink to size 1 on every new character encountered (since adding any second 'b' always creates a duplicate), so the longest valid window never exceeds length 1.

syntax_mcq.question: In `windowSum += nums[right]; windowSum -= nums[right - k];`, what is this pair of operations accomplishing together?
options: It computes the sum of the entire array from scratch each time

It efficiently slides the window forward by ONE position: adding the newly-entering element (at position right) and removing the element that just exited the window (at position right - k), avoiding the need to re-sum the entire window from scratch
It deletes elements from the original array
It has no effect on windowSum
syntax_mcq.explanation: This is the core O(1)-per-step sliding mechanism for fixed windows: rather than recomputing the sum of all k elements in the new window position, you incrementally update the running sum by adding the one new element and subtracting the one element that's no longer in the window.

coding_challenges.title: Sliding Window Toolkit: Fixed and Variable
coding_challenges.problem_statement: Implement both a fixed-size and a variable-size sliding window solution, then build a window-event tracer that logs every expand/shrink operation to visually confirm the O(n) total-movement claim.
requirements: Implement `maxSumSubarrayK(nums, k)` matching the lesson's fixed-window approach
Implement `longestSubstringNoRepeat(s)` matching the lesson's variable-window approach

Implement `traceWindowEvents(s)` that runs the variable-window algorithm on a string and returns `{ totalExpands, totalShrinks }`, where totalExpands should equal s.length (right moves exactly once per character) and totalShrinks should never exceed s.length (left moves at most once per character total, confirming the O(n) amortized claim)
coding_challenges.complexity_analysis: maxSumSubarrayK: O(n) time, O(1) space. longestSubstringNoRepeat: O(n) time, O(min(n, alphabet_size)) space. traceWindowEvents empirically confirms totalExpands = s.length always, and totalShrinks <= s.length always, proving the combined while-loop work across the entire run is bounded by O(n), not O(n) per outer iteration.

hints.text: maxSumSubarrayK: build the first window's sum, then slide by adding the new right element and subtracting the element that just left.
longestSubstringNoRepeat: use a Set to track characters currently in the window; shrink from the left whenever the new right character is already present.
traceWindowEvents mirrors longestSubstringNoRepeat exactly but increments totalExpands once per outer iteration and totalShrinks once per while-loop iteration.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the prefix sum array use a 'dummy zero' at index 0 (making it length n+1 rather than length n)?
options: It's purely stylistic and has no functional purpose

The dummy zero avoids off-by-one edge cases — specifically, it allows the range sum formula prefix[r+1] - prefix[l] to work correctly even when l=0, without needing a special-case check for the start of the array
It makes the array exactly double the original size
It is required by JavaScript syntax
theory_mcq.explanation: Without the dummy zero, computing sum(0, r) would require a special case (since there'd be no prefix[-1] to subtract). With prefix[0]=0 representing 'sum of zero elements', the formula prefix[r+1]-prefix[l] works uniformly for ANY valid l, including l=0, eliminating the edge case entirely.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the prefix sum approach dramatically outperform repeated linear scans when answering MULTIPLE range sum queries on the same static array?
options: It doesn't actually outperform repeated scans

Without prefix sums, k queries each cost O(n), totaling O(n×k); with prefix sums, a single O(n) preprocessing pass enables each subsequent query to run in O(1), totaling O(n + k) — a substantial improvement when k is large
Prefix sums only work for k=1 query
Prefix sums require rebuilding the array before every single query
theory_mcq.explanation: This matches the lesson's explicit complexity comparison: O(n×k) without prefix sums versus O(n+k) with them — the gap grows dramatically as the number of queries k increases, which is exactly the scenario prefix sums are designed for.

logic_mcq.question: Given arr=[3,1,4,1,5,9,2,6] and its prefix array [0,3,4,8,9,14,23,25,31], what is rangeSum(prefix, 2, 5), and does it match a direct sum of arr[2..5]?
options: rangeSum returns 14, but the direct sum of arr[2..5] is 19 — a mismatch
rangeSum returns prefix[6]-prefix[2] = 23-4 = 19, which matches the direct sum arr[2]+arr[3]+arr[4]+arr[5] = 4+1+5+9 = 19
rangeSum returns 23, an incorrect calculation
This combination of indices is invalid
logic_mcq.explanation: This is the lesson's own worked example: rangeSum(prefix, 2, 5) = prefix[5+1] - prefix[2] = prefix[6] - prefix[2] = 23 - 4 = 19, which correctly matches the direct calculation 4+1+5+9=19, verifying the formula's correctness.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `subarraySum([1,1,1], k=2)` using the lesson's prefix-sum-plus-hashmap approach. What count is returned, and which subarrays does it represent?
options: Returns 1, representing only [1,1] at indices 0-1
Returns 2, representing the subarrays [1,1] at indices 0-1 AND [1,1] at indices 1-2 — both sum to 2
Returns 3, counting every possible subarray regardless of sum
Returns 0, since no subarray sums to exactly 2
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact trace: prefix sums are 0,1,2,3. At running sum=2 (after index 1), countMap had seen sum=0 once (the initial dummy entry), contributing count=1. At running sum=3 (after index 2), countMap had seen sum=1 once (from index 0), contributing another count, total=2. This corresponds to the two overlapping subarrays [1,1] at indices [0,1] and [1,2], both summing to 2.

logic_mcq.question: Why does `subarraySum` initialize `countMap` with `new Map([[0, 1]])` rather than an empty Map?
options: This is an arbitrary, unnecessary initialization

It accounts for the case where a prefix sum EXACTLY equals k from the very start of the array (an 'empty prefix' before any elements, representing sum=0, must be counted as having been seen once) — without this, subarrays starting at index 0 that sum to exactly k would be undercounted
It sets a maximum limit of 1 on all counts
It is required to avoid a syntax error
logic_mcq.explanation: The comment in the lesson's code explains this directly: 'prefix sum 0 was seen once (empty prefix)' — this ensures that if a subarray starting at index 0 sums to exactly k (so prefixSum - k = 0), it's correctly counted, since 0 is registered as having occurred once before any elements are processed.

syntax_mcq.question: In `count += countMap.get(prefixSum - k) || 0;`, what does the `|| 0` accomplish?
options: It always adds 0 to count, making this line useless

It provides a fallback default of 0 when `countMap.get(prefixSum - k)` returns `undefined` (i.e., that key doesn't exist in the Map) — since undefined can't be meaningfully added to count, this ensures count only increases by an actual found value or by 0 if not found
It deletes the key from the Map after reading it
It converts count to a boolean
syntax_mcq.explanation: `Map.get()` returns `undefined` for a missing key. `undefined || 0` evaluates to `0` (since undefined is falsy), providing a safe default — this idiom prevents `count` from becoming NaN when prefixSum - k hasn't been seen yet.

Add a comment demonstrating, with your own numbers, why this approach beats naively summing each range query directly when there are many queries

theory_mcq.question: Why does building a string via repeated concatenation in a loop (`result += c`) become O(n²), even though it looks like a simple O(n) loop?
options: Because loops are always O(n²) in JavaScript

Because strings are immutable — each `+=` operation must allocate an entirely NEW string and copy all previously accumulated characters into it, so the total copying work across n iterations sums to 0+1+2+...+(n-1) = O(n²)
Because concatenation is a deprecated operation
It is actually O(n), not O(n²); the lesson's claim is incorrect
theory_mcq.explanation: Since strings can't be mutated in place, each concatenation creates a new string copy of everything accumulated so far PLUS the new character. Summed across n iterations, this produces a triangular-number total of copied characters, giving O(n²) overall despite the deceptively simple-looking loop.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the array-push-then-join pattern (`parts.push(c)` then `parts.join('')`) achieve O(n) total time, fixing the concatenation problem?
options: Because array push is always instant with zero cost

Because pushing to an array is O(1) amortized per operation (no copying of all previous content each time, unlike string concatenation), and the single final .join() call does one O(n) pass to build the final string — giving O(n) total instead of O(n²)
Because arrays and strings are identical data structures internally
This pattern is actually slower than direct concatenation
theory_mcq.explanation: Array push doesn't require copying all prior elements (it's amortized O(1), per L1's dynamic array lesson) — accumulating n elements this way is O(n) total. The final .join() does exactly one pass over all elements, O(n). Combined: O(n) + O(n) = O(n), versus the O(n²) of repeated string concatenation.

logic_mcq.question: In `countLetters`, why is `c.charCodeAt(0) - 97` used to compute the array index for a given lowercase character?
options: This is an arbitrary, meaningless calculation

Since 'a' has ASCII code 97, subtracting 97 from any lowercase letter's char code maps 'a'->0, 'b'->1, ..., 'z'->25, exactly matching the indices of a 26-element array representing each letter of the alphabet
It converts the character to uppercase
It always returns 0 regardless of the input character
logic_mcq.explanation: This is the ASCII arithmetic trick the lesson demonstrates: 'a'=97, so any lowercase letter's char code minus 97 gives its zero-indexed position in the alphabet (a=0, b=1, ..., z=25), which directly maps to indices in a 26-element frequency array without needing a hash map.

logic_mcq.question: What does `countLetters('aab')` return, tracing through the function?
options: [2,1,0,...,0] — index 0 ('a') is incremented twice (count=2), index 1 ('b') is incremented once (count=1), all other 24 indices remain 0
An error, since the function doesn't handle repeated characters
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact stated result: 'a' appears twice (incrementing index 0 to 2), 'b' appears once (incrementing index 1 to 1), and the remaining 24 letters of the alphabet are never encountered, staying at their initial value of 0.

syntax_mcq.question: What does `parts.join('')` do when `parts` is an array of single characters?
options: It sorts the array alphabetically
It concatenates all elements of the array into a single string, with no separator between them (since the join argument is an empty string), producing the final assembled string in one O(n) operation
It reverses the array
It returns the array unchanged as an array
syntax_mcq.explanation: `.join(separator)` concatenates all array elements into a single string, inserting the given separator between each pair. With an empty string `''` as the separator, elements are joined directly with nothing between them, producing a plain concatenated string.

syntax_mcq.question: In `s.split('')`, what does this expression do to a string `s`, and why is it necessary before reversing a string with the two-pointer pattern?
options: It deletes the string entirely

It converts the string into an array of individual characters; this is necessary because strings are immutable in JavaScript and cannot be modified in-place by swapping characters, so an array copy is required to perform in-place-style swaps
It capitalizes every character
It has no functional effect
syntax_mcq.explanation: Since JS strings can't be mutated character-by-character directly, `.split('')` creates a mutable array copy of the characters, on which the two-pointer swap technique (`[arr[left], arr[right]] = [arr[right], arr[left]]`) can actually operate, before rejoining into a final string.

theory_mcq.question: Why does `isAnagram` use a single 26-element array, incrementing for one string and decrementing for the other, rather than two separate frequency maps?
options: It is purely a stylistic preference with no efficiency benefit

Using one shared array and incrementing/decrementing means that if both strings have IDENTICAL character frequencies, every count returns to exactly 0 — a single, simple final check (`count.every(c => c === 0)`) confirms the anagram relationship without needing to compare two separate arrays element-by-element
It uses less memory than any other possible approach
Two separate frequency maps would produce incorrect results
theory_mcq.explanation: This is an elegant simplification: by incrementing for string s and decrementing for string t on the SAME array, matching frequencies cancel out to zero. If they're true anagrams, every position ends at 0; if not, at least one position will be nonzero, both checked with one simple .every() call instead of comparing two separate arrays.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the lesson note 'Character map vs sorting: O(n) vs O(n log n)' as a meaningful comparison for anagram detection?
options: Sorting and character maps always have identical complexity

Sorting both strings and comparing them (an alternative anagram-detection approach) costs O(n log n) due to the sort step, while a character-frequency-array approach (fixed 26-element alphabet) achieves O(n) — a real, meaningful complexity improvement when frequent anagram checks matter
Sorting is always faster than character maps
This distinction only matters for strings longer than 1 million characters
theory_mcq.explanation: An alternative correct approach (sort each string and compare) costs O(n log n) due to the sorting step. The character-frequency-array approach in this lesson achieves a strictly better O(n), since it relies on a single linear pass with O(1) array indexing rather than a comparison-based sort.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `isAnagram('rat', 'car')`. What happens to count[r-97] (the index for 'r'), and what does this reveal about the final result?
options: count[r-97] ends at 0, same as all other indices

count[r-97] is incremented once (from 'rat') but never decremented (since 'car' contains no 'r'), leaving it at +1 — this nonzero value means count.every(c => c === 0) returns false, correctly identifying 'rat' and 'car' as NOT anagrams
count[r-97] is decremented to -1
The function throws an error for this input
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's stated result: 'rat' increments r's count, but 'car' (r,a,c... wait, car has no 'r') never decrements it back, leaving count[r-97]=+1, which is nonzero — correctly signaling that these strings are not anagrams since their character sets differ.

logic_mcq.question: In `groupAnagrams(['eat','tea','tan','ate','nat','bat'])`, why do 'eat', 'tea', and 'ate' all map to the same key, while 'tan' and 'nat' map to a different shared key?
options: Because all six strings happen to be the same length

Because sorting each string's characters alphabetically produces a canonical 'fingerprint' — 'eat','tea','ate' all sort to 'aet', while 'tan' and 'nat' both sort to 'ant' — so anagrams of each other always produce the identical sorted-key, grouping them together in the Map regardless of original character order
Because the Map randomly assigns keys
Because 'eat', 'tea', and 'ate' are not actually anagrams
logic_mcq.explanation: This is the lesson's exact worked example: sorting each string's characters produces a canonical representation that's identical for all anagrams of each other ('eat'->'aet', 'tea'->'aet', 'ate'->'aet'), which is precisely why the sorted string works as a grouping key in the Map.

logic_mcq.question: In `findAnagrams('cbaebabacd', 'abc')`, the result is `[0, 6]`. What does each of these indices represent?
options: Random positions with no meaning

Index 0 means the substring starting at position 0 ('cba') is an anagram of 'abc'; index 6 means the substring starting at position 6 ('bac') is also an anagram of 'abc' — these are the starting positions of every length-3 substring of s that's an anagram of p
These indices represent the length of the string
Both indices represent the same substring counted twice
logic_mcq.explanation: findAnagrams returns the STARTING indices of every substring in s with the same length as p that is a character-frequency match (anagram) of p — here, s[0:3]='cba' and s[6:9]='bac' are both rearrangements of 'abc', matching the function's stated result.

syntax_mcq.question: In `pCount.join() === wCount.join()`, why does comparing the joined string representations work as a way to check if two frequency arrays are equal?
options: This comparison is actually incorrect and will give wrong results

`.join()` converts each array into a comma-separated string (e.g., [2,0,1] -> '2,0,1'); two arrays produce IDENTICAL joined strings if and only if they have the same elements in the same positions, so comparing the joined strings is a correct (if not maximally efficient) way to check array equality
join() sorts the array before converting to a string
This only works for arrays containing strings, not numbers
syntax_mcq.explanation: `.join()` with no separator argument defaults to a comma, converting the array into a deterministic string representation. Since two equal arrays produce identical strings, comparing the join() results is a valid (though not the most performant) way to check array equality position-by-position.

theory_mcq.question: What is the core insight behind Kadane's Algorithm that allows it to find the maximum subarray sum in O(n) time?
options: It checks every possible subarray individually but very quickly

At each position, the algorithm decides whether to EXTEND the current subarray (if doing so increases the sum) or START FRESH from the current element (if the accumulated sum has become a net negative drag) — this local greedy decision, made once per element, provably leads to the global maximum without needing to examine every subarray explicitly
It only works on arrays containing exclusively positive numbers
It sorts the array first, then sums the largest elements
theory_mcq.explanation: Kadane's core insight, shown in `currentSum = Math.max(nums[i], currentSum + nums[i])`: at each step, decide whether the running sum so far is still helping (extend) or has become a net negative (start fresh at the current element) — this single O(1) decision per element, repeated n times, finds the global maximum in O(n) total.

theory_mcq.question: Why must `maxProduct` track BOTH a running maximum AND a running minimum product, unlike Kadane's sum version which only needs a running maximum?
options: Tracking the minimum is unnecessary; this is an error in the lesson

Because multiplying by a NEGATIVE number can flip a very negative (small) product into a very positive (large) one — so the current minimum product is a candidate for becoming the NEW maximum if the next number is negative, which sum-based Kadane's doesn't need to worry about since addition doesn't have this sign-flipping property
Because product calculations are always twice as expensive as sum calculations
Because arrays with products always have exactly two valid answers
theory_mcq.explanation: This is the lesson's key distinguishing insight for the product variant: unlike addition, multiplication by a negative number can turn the smallest (most negative) running product into the largest (most positive) one — so you must track both extremes at every step, since either could become the new maximum depending on the sign of the next number.

logic_mcq.question: Trace Kadane's algorithm on `[-2,1,-3,4,-1,2,1,-5,4]`. According to the lesson's trace, what is the final answer, and which subarray produces it?
options: Answer: 6, from subarray [4,-1,2,1]
Answer: -2, from the first element alone
Answer: 15, the sum of all positive numbers
Answer: 4, from the single element 4
logic_mcq.explanation: This is the lesson's own worked trace, with maxSum reaching 6 at the point where currentSum accumulates through [4,-1,2,1] = 4-1+2+1 = 6, which is indeed the maximum subarray sum for this input as explicitly stated in the lesson.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `maxProduct([-2,3,-4])`. Why does the result end up being 24 (the product of ALL elements), rather than just 3 (the largest single positive number)?
options: This is incorrect; the actual answer should be 3

Because the two negative numbers (-2 and -4) multiply together to produce a positive 8, and combined with 3, the full-array product -2×3×-4=24 is larger than any partial product — this is exactly the scenario the min-tracking logic is designed to catch, since a running minimum (very negative) can become the new maximum once multiplied by another negative
Because the algorithm always returns the product of the entire array regardless of values
Because 24 is simply incorrect output from a buggy algorithm
logic_mcq.explanation: This matches the lesson's stated result exactly: two negatives multiplying to a positive means the FULL array's product (24) beats any subset, and this is precisely why tracking the running minimum (which captures the most-negative running product) is essential — it can flip to become the new maximum when multiplied by a subsequent negative number.

logic_mcq.question: Per the lesson's pattern selection guide, a problem asking for 'the minimum SIZE subarray with sum at least target, given all POSITIVE numbers' should use which technique?
options: Kadane's algorithm

Sliding window — since the constraint mentions a size requirement on a contiguous subarray with positive numbers (meaning the window sum changes monotonically as it expands/shrinks), matching the lesson's explicit recognition signal: 'Min SIZE with sum >= target, POSITIVE -> sliding window O(n)'
Prefix sum + hashmap
Matrix traversal
logic_mcq.explanation: This exactly matches the lesson's stated pattern selection guide entry: 'Min SIZE with sum >= target, POSITIVE numbers -> sliding window O(n)' — the all-positive constraint is what makes the window's sum behave monotonically, enabling the sliding window technique to work correctly.

syntax_mcq.question: In `const candidates = [num, maxProd * num, minProd * num]; maxProd = Math.max(...candidates);`, what does the spread operator `...` accomplish?
options: It creates a copy of the candidates array without changing anything

It expands the array `candidates` into individual arguments, so `Math.max(...candidates)` is equivalent to `Math.max(candidates[0], candidates[1], candidates[2])` — necessary because Math.max expects individual number arguments, not an array
It deletes the candidates array after use
It converts the array to a string
syntax_mcq.explanation: `Math.max()` doesn't accept an array directly — it expects comma-separated arguments. The spread operator `...candidates` unpacks the array's elements as individual arguments, allowing `Math.max(...candidates)` to correctly find the maximum among all three candidate values.

Implement `maxProductSubarray(nums)` tracking both max and min running products

maxProductSubarray: at each step, compute all three candidates (current number alone, max*current, min*current), then take the max and min of those three as the new running max/min.
minSubArrayLen: expand the window by adding nums[right]; whenever sum >= target, record the window length and shrink from the left while still valid.

theory_mcq.question: Why does row-major traversal have 'good cache locality' while column-major traversal is described as slower in practice, even though both are O(m×n)?
options: Cache locality has no real performance impact

Row-major traversal accesses elements that are contiguous in memory (since 2D arrays are typically stored row-by-row internally), which the CPU's cache can prefetch efficiently; column-major traversal jumps across rows for each step, accessing memory locations far apart, causing more cache misses despite doing the same total NUMBER of operations
Column-major traversal does strictly more operations than row-major
This distinction only applies to matrices larger than 1000x1000
theory_mcq.explanation: Both traversal orders are O(m×n) in raw operation count, but row-major traversal matches how 2D arrays are typically laid out in memory (row-by-row), giving good cache locality (sequential access). Column-major traversal accesses memory in a scattered pattern, causing more cache misses — same Big O, but meaningfully different real-world performance due to memory access patterns.

theory_mcq.question: Why is bounds checking (`r >= 0 && r < m && c >= 0 && c < n`) always necessary when computing a neighbor's position in a matrix?
options: Bounds checking is optional and only a defensive best practice

Without bounds checking, computing a neighbor at the edge or corner of the matrix (e.g., row=0 checking 'up') would produce an out-of-bounds index, which could cause incorrect behavior or runtime errors — checking ensures only valid, in-grid positions are considered
Bounds checking only matters for square matrices
JavaScript automatically prevents all out-of-bounds access
theory_mcq.explanation: Edge and corner cells have fewer than 4 valid neighbors (e.g., the top-left corner has only 2: right and down). Without explicit bounds checking, the directional offset calculation would compute invalid row/column indices for non-existent neighbors, which must be filtered out before use.

logic_mcq.question: Using `DIRS = [[0,1],[0,-1],[1,0],[-1,0]]` (right, left, down, up), what are the valid neighbors of position (0, 0) in a 3x3 matrix?
options: All four directions are valid: (0,1), (0,-1), (1,0), (-1,0)
Only 2 directions are valid: (0,1) [right] and (1,0) [down] — since (0,-1) [left] and (-1,0) [up] would both produce a negative index, which fails the bounds check (r >= 0 && c >= 0)
Only 1 direction is valid
No directions are valid from the corner
logic_mcq.explanation: From (0,0), moving left would give column -1 (invalid) and moving up would give row -1 (invalid) — both fail the `>= 0` bounds check. Only right (0,1) and down (1,0) produce valid, in-bounds positions, confirming that corner cells have exactly 2 neighbors in this 4-directional scheme.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `spiralOrder` on a 3x3 matrix [[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]]. What is the resulting order, following the lesson's top-right-bottom-left pattern?
options: 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 (simple row-major order)
1,2,3,6,9,8,7,4,5 — top row left-to-right, then right column top-to-bottom, then bottom row right-to-left, then left column bottom-to-top, then the remaining center element
1,4,7,2,5,8,3,6,9 (column-major order)
logic_mcq.explanation: Tracing the spiral: top row (1,2,3) left-to-right, then right column (6,9) top-to-bottom (skipping 3, already visited), then bottom row (8,7) right-to-left (skipping 9), then left column (4) bottom-to-top (skipping 7), then the center (5) remains — giving 1,2,3,6,9,8,7,4,5, matching the standard spiral traversal pattern this lesson implements.

logic_mcq.question: In the in-place rotation function, why does the algorithm perform a TRANSPOSE first, then REVERSE each row, rather than directly computing each element's final rotated position?
options: This two-step approach is unnecessarily complicated and a single-step approach doesn't exist

Transpose-then-reverse-rows is a well-known decomposition that achieves a 90-degree clockwise rotation using only simple, easy-to-verify O(1)-space operations (swapping pairs across the diagonal, then reversing rows in place) — avoiding the need to allocate a separate output matrix or carefully derive a single complex index-mapping formula
This approach actually rotates the matrix 180 degrees, not 90
Transpose alone is sufficient; the row reversal step is redundant
logic_mcq.explanation: The transpose-then-reverse-rows technique is a standard, provably-correct decomposition: transposing swaps the matrix across its main diagonal, and then reversing each row completes the 90-degree clockwise rotation — both steps are simple in-place operations (O(1) extra space), avoiding the complexity of deriving and implementing a direct index-mapping formula for each element's final position.

syntax_mcq.question: In `for (const [dr, dc] of DIRS) { const r = row + dr, c = col + dc; ... }`, what does the destructuring `[dr, dc]` accomplish within the for-of loop?
options: It creates a new array on every iteration with no purpose

Since DIRS is an array of [rowDelta, colDelta] pairs, this destructures each pair directly into the named variables `dr` and `dc` during iteration, making the subsequent calculation `row + dr, col + dc` clear and readable without needing to index into each pair manually (e.g., avoiding `dir[0]`, `dir[1]`)
It filters out invalid directions automatically
It sorts the DIRS array before iterating
syntax_mcq.explanation: This is array destructuring applied within a for-of loop: each element of DIRS (itself a 2-element array like [0,1]) is unpacked directly into `dr` and `dc`, avoiding the need for manual indexing (`dir[0]`, `dir[1]`) and making the neighbor-offset calculation more readable.

syntax_mcq.question: What does `matrix[i].reverse()` do, called inside a loop over each row index `i`?
options: It reverses the entire matrix (all rows), not just one row
It reverses the elements WITHIN the i-th row in place (Array.prototype.reverse() mutates the array it's called on), which is the second step of the transpose-then-reverse 90-degree rotation technique
It deletes the i-th row entirely
It creates a new matrix without modifying the original
syntax_mcq.explanation: `.reverse()` is an in-place array method that reverses the order of elements within the array it's called on. Called as `matrix[i].reverse()`, it reverses just the i-th row's elements, which combined with the prior transpose step completes the 90-degree clockwise rotation.

coding_challenges.complexity_analysis: getNeighboursImpl: O(1) (fixed 4 directions checked). spiralOrderImpl: O(m×n) time, O(1) extra space (excluding output). rotateImpl: O(n²) time, O(1) extra space — purely in-place, no new matrix allocated.

hints.text: getNeighboursImpl: for each [dr,dc] in DIRS, compute the candidate position and check it's within [0, m) and [0, n).

spiralOrderImpl: maintain four shrinking boundaries (top, bottom, left, right) and traverse top row, right column, bottom row, left column in sequence, with guards to avoid double-processing the center row/column.
rotateImpl: first swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i] for all j>i (transpose), then call .reverse() on each row.

theory_mcq.question: What is the purpose of the 'pattern selection decision tree' introduced in this lesson?
options: To memorize the solution to every specific LeetCode problem individually

To build a structured, reusable mapping from PROBLEM SIGNALS (phrases like 'sorted array + pair', 'longest contiguous + constraint', 'count subarrays with sum') to the CORRECT underlying pattern (Two Pointers, Sliding Window, Prefix Sum, etc.), enabling fast pattern recognition on NEW, previously unseen problems
To replace the need for understanding any individual pattern in depth
To only apply to problems explicitly labeled with their pattern name
theory_mcq.explanation: This lesson's explicit goal, consistent with L1-M01's broader philosophy, is building a transferable RECOGNITION skill: mapping problem language signals to underlying patterns, so unfamiliar problems can be solved by recognizing which of the ~5 techniques from this module applies, rather than requiring prior exposure to that exact problem.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the lesson explicitly note 'when brute force is the intended solution (small n constraints)' as part of the decision process?
options: Brute force is never an acceptable interview answer

Sometimes the input size constraints given in a problem (e.g., n <= 20) are small enough that an O(n²) or even O(2^n) brute force is intentionally acceptable, and over-engineering an unnecessarily complex optimal solution wastes time when the simpler approach is both correct and sufficient for the given constraints
Brute force is always faster than any optimized pattern
This consideration only applies to string problems, never arrays
theory_mcq.explanation: Recognizing input size constraints is part of practical pattern selection: a problem explicitly bounding n to a small value (e.g., n <= 20) signals that an exponential or quadratic brute force is the EXPECTED solution, and reaching for unnecessary optimization in that case can waste interview time without adding value.

logic_mcq.question: A problem states: 'Given an array, find the longest contiguous subarray where the count of zeros is at most k.' Applying the lesson's decision tree, which pattern should be selected, and why?
options: Two Pointers (opposite ends), because the problem mentions an array

Variable Sliding Window, because the signal 'longest...contiguous' + 'at most k' (a constraint) exactly matches the lesson's stated recognition signal: 'longest/shortest contiguous + constraint -> VARIABLE SLIDING WINDOW'
Prefix Sum, because zeros need to be counted
Matrix Traversal, because the problem involves an array
logic_mcq.explanation: This is the lesson's own worked example (longestSubarrayKZeros): the phrase 'longest...contiguous' combined with the 'at most k' constraint directly matches the variable sliding window recognition signal, which is exactly the pattern the lesson's example function implements.

logic_mcq.question: Per the lesson's Blind 75 mapping, 'Product of Array Except Self' (id 238) is tagged with pattern 'Prefix Sum variant.' Based on what you know about prefix sums from L5, why might this specific problem be considered a VARIANT rather than a standard prefix sum application?
options: Because it has nothing to do with prefix sums at all

Because standard prefix sums (L5) compute running SUMS for range-sum queries, while this problem requires computing running PRODUCTS (prefix products from the left, and suffix products from the right, multiplied together per position) — the same underlying technique (precompute left-to-right, then combine with right-to-left) applied to a different operation than the sum-based examples in L5
Because it uses sliding window exclusively, with no relation to prefix sums
Because it can only be solved with Kadane's algorithm
logic_mcq.explanation: While L5 demonstrated prefix SUMS specifically, the underlying technique generalizes: precomputing a running aggregate from one direction (and often from the other direction too) to answer per-position queries efficiently is the same conceptual pattern applied here to PRODUCTS instead of sums, justifying its classification as a 'variant' of the prefix sum technique.

syntax_mcq.question: In `while (zeros > k) { if (nums[left++] === 0) zeros--; }`, what does the combined `nums[left++]` expression accomplish?
options: It only increments left without accessing the array

It reads the value at the CURRENT value of `left` (using it in the comparison `=== 0`), AND THEN increments `left` by one, all in a single expression — this is the post-increment operator combined with array access, advancing the window's left boundary while checking the value being removed
It is invalid JavaScript syntax
It deletes the element at index left
syntax_mcq.explanation: The post-increment operator `left++` returns the CURRENT value of `left` for use in the expression (here, as the array index), and only AFTER that increments the variable. So `nums[left++]` reads `nums[left]` first, then increments `left` — combining the 'check the value being removed from the window' and 'advance the left boundary' into one compact line.

coding_challenges.title: Capstone Project: Array Pattern Auto-Selector and Solver
coding_challenges.project_style: freeCodeCamp-style capstone project — synthesizes concepts from ALL 10 lessons in this module
coding_challenges.problem_statement: Build a tool that takes a structured problem descriptor (signals extracted from a problem statement) and both SELECTS the correct pattern AND solves a representative problem using that pattern, demonstrating mastery of all five core techniques from this module (Two Pointers, Sliding Window, Prefix Sum, Character Map, Kadane's) plus matrix traversal awareness.
requirements: Implement `detectPattern(signals)` taking an array of signal strings (e.g., ['sorted', 'pair_sum']) and returning the matching pattern name, using the lesson's recognition signal table (at minimum handle: sorted+pair->'Two Pointers', longest+constraint->'Sliding Window', range_sum_query->'Prefix Sum', anagram->'Character Map', max_subarray_sum->'Kadane')

Implement `solveWithDetectedPattern(problemType, input)` that calls detectPattern internally based on problemType, then dispatches to and returns the result of the appropriate solver function from this module's other challenges (you may reimplement minimal versions inline)

Implement `moduleSelfCheck()` returning an object summarizing which of the 5 core patterns have at least one working solver wired up, e.g. `{ twoPointers: true, slidingWindow: true, prefixSum: true, characterMap: true, kadane: true }`
Write a comment block documenting, in your own words, the recognition signal for EACH of the 5 patterns, mirroring this lesson's cheat sheet
coding_challenges.complexity_analysis: detectPattern: O(1) (fixed-size signal checking). solveWithDetectedPattern dispatches to the underlying pattern's own complexity (e.g., O(n) for the two-pointer two-sum solver). This capstone demonstrates the META-skill of pattern selection itself, building on top of the concrete implementations from lessons 1-9.

hints.text: detectPattern: convert signals to a Set for O(1) membership checks, then apply if/else checks matching the lesson's recognition table.

solveWithDetectedPattern doesn't need to call detectPattern for every possible problemType in this exercise — focus on wiring up at least one working example end-to-end (e.g., two_sum_sorted) to demonstrate the dispatch pattern.
moduleSelfCheck can simply return a static object confirming each pattern has working code somewhere in this file, or dynamically check that the corresponding solver functions are defined.
